summary: Defines an optional extension to RELOAD to support relay peer routing. It gives responses a shorter route and reduces overhead on intermediate peers.

eli5.summary: In a chain of friends passing notes, one friend can act as a shortcut so the reply gets back faster, and fewer friends are kept busy.

questions: what is a relay peer in p2psip
subtitle: Lets a RELOAD response take a shortcut through a relay peer instead of retracing the whole request path.

tldr.problem: RELOAD normally sends a response back along the reverse of the request path (symmetric recursive routing), which loads every intermediate peer and takes many hops.
tldr.mechanism: The sending peer names a publicly reachable relay peer inside the request. The destination peer sends the response to that relay peer, which forwards it straight to the sender over an existing connection.
tldr.outcome: Responses use a shorter route and put less load on intermediate peers, but RPR is optional and peers must still support the older routing mode as a fallback.

today: RFC 7264 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It builds on RFC 6940 and sits beside the DRR extension in RFC 7263.

sections.title: Why Responses Need a Shortcut
sections.content:
The RELOAD base protocol (RFC 6940) recommends symmetric recursive routing (SRR): a response retraces the request's path in reverse. Appendix A of that RFC also discusses two alternatives, direct response routing (DRR) and relay peer routing (RPR). This document specifies RPR as a standalone extension; RFC 7263 covers DRR.

The RFC argues that RPR can reduce CPU and link bandwidth load on intermediate peers. It works best where relay peers are provisioned in advance and are publicly reachable. Elsewhere, combining RPR with SRR is more likely to help than SRR alone.
sections.eli5: Normally a reply walks back through every friend who passed the note along. RPR lets the reply jump through one helper friend instead, so the others do not have to carry it.

sections.title: How Relay Peer Routing Works
sections.content:
A relay peer is a publicly reachable peer that can receive unsolicited messages from all other peers in the overlay and forward responses toward the sender of the request. If peer A is behind a NAT and has a prior connection to relay peer R, A puts R's transport address in the request. When the destination peer X receives it, X sends the response to R, and R forwards it to A on the existing connection.

Peers using RPR MUST maintain a connection with their relay peers, for example by using the Attach method from RFC 6940. The request MUST also carry the requester's Node-ID or IP address so the relay can route the response to the right peer. A relay peer needs no extra functionality beyond an ordinary peer; the difference is that it may carry more traffic, and it can decide whether to accept a new connection based on its current load.

Peers need a way to learn which peers can be relays. The RFC suggests an initial relay list in the overlay configuration, or a response message in which a peer announces that it can act as a relay.
sections.eli5: You tell the far-away friend, "Send your answer to my helper, and my helper will hand it to me." The helper already knows how to reach you.

sections.title: Where RPR Fits and Where It Does Not
sections.content:
The RFC lists three settings. In managed or closed P2P systems, an administrator can deploy publicly reachable relay peers and list them in the configuration file; peers behind NATs then use them. Relays can also sit on the managed network boundary. Bootstrap nodes are typically publicly reachable, so they are well suited to be relays. In some mobile deployments, RPR may reduce radio battery use and bandwidth for intermediate peers.

RPR is not meant to replace SRR. Peers MUST also support SRR in case RPR fails. If the service provider supplies a relay peer, peers SHOULD prefer RPR over SRR. However, RPR SHOULD NOT be used in the open Internet or when the administrator lacks enough information about the overlay topology. All peers MUST be able to process SRR requests and MAY support RPR.
sections.eli5: The shortcut works best in a club where the helpers are set up ahead of time. In a huge open crowd you cannot be sure a helper will be there, so you keep the old way as a backup.

sections.title: The Routing Option in the Request
sections.content:
RPR adds a new value to the RouteMode enum from RFC 7263: RPR(2). It is carried in the ExtensiveRoutingModeOption structure, which holds routemode, transport (the transport type used to deliver the response to the relay), ipaddressport (the relay's transport address) and destinations.

To use RPR, the sending peer MUST set the IGNORE-STATE-KEEPING flag in the ForwardingHeader and include a ForwardingOption whose type is extensive_routing_mode. Inside it, routemode is 0x02, and destinations MUST hold exactly two node entries: first the relay peer, then the sending peer itself.
sections.eli5: The request carries a small label that says "use the helper", gives the helper's address, and names both the helper and the sender.

sections.title: Handling Requests and Responses
sections.content:
When the destination peer sees an RPR option, it MUST build a destination_list for the response with two entries: the relay peer's Node-ID first, then the sending peer's Node-ID. It sends the response to the address in ipaddressport, using the transport named in the option.

If the destination does not understand the extensive_routing_mode option, or RPR is requested without exactly two destinations, it MUST try to return an Error_Unknown_Extension response using SRR. If it receives a retransmit that prefers SRR, it SHOULD abort the RPR response and use SRR.

The relay peer follows the normal RFC 6940 rules: it validates the message, adjusts the destination_list and forwards to the next hop using its connection table. The only difference from SRR is that the list is built from the forwarding option, not from the reverse of the via_list. If the sender gets no response before the timeout, it MAY retry with RPR through a different relay, or with SRR.
sections.eli5: The answering friend sends the reply to the helper first. If it does not work out, the sender can try another helper or just use the old long way.

sections.title: Configuration and Finding Relay Peers
sections.content:
The overlay configuration uses the route-mode element inside each configuration element, as defined in RFC 7263. For this document the route mode MUST be RPR.

Relay peers can be advertised in several ways: listed in the configuration file by the network provider, advertised through a service discovery mechanism (the RFC mentions the one used for TURN server discovery in RFC 6940), or announced by a peer in its response to an Attach or Join. Appendix A adds optional methods for a peer to check whether it is publicly reachable, and notes there is no foolproof way to tell other than out-of-band mechanisms.
sections.eli5: Helpers can be written on a list the club hands out, or a friend can say "I can be a helper" when they reply to you.

sections.title: Cost Compared with SRR
sections.content:
Appendix B compares hops and messages. For a response in a closed network, SRR takes log(N) hops and log(N) messages, while RPR takes 2 hops and 2 messages. With DTLS to the relay, RPR needs 7+2 messages. RPR uses fewer hops than SRR in most cases where the number of peers N is greater than 4, and fewer messages when N is greater than 512. When N is below 512 it uses more messages, so the choice depends on how much intermediate-peer resource matters.

In open networks, a failed RPR attempt that falls back to SRR costs 2+log(N) hops. The RFC still concludes that trying RPR first can give fewer hops overall than going directly to SRR.
sections.eli5: The shortcut is always two steps, while the long way gets longer as the crowd grows. For a small crowd, setting up the helper can cost more chatter, so it pays off most in big groups.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The security recommendations of Section 13 of RFC 6940 apply. RPR behaves like a DRR requesting node toward the destination node. The relay peer should be a trusted node, such as one in a managed network, a bootstrap node or a configured relay. To address possible DoS attacks, the relay peer SHOULD also limit its maximum number of connections.

IANA registered one new RELOAD Forwarding Option: code 2, extensive_routing_mode.
sections.eli5: You should pick a helper you trust, and a helper should not take on more friends than it can handle.
